questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish modularity from reuse?
options: They are exactly the same quality with two different names
Reuse always requires sacrificing modularity

Modularity is how cleanly a solution is broken into independent, well-bounded pieces; reuse is whether those pieces actually get consumed in more than one place -- modularity makes reuse possible but doesn't guarantee it happens
Modularity only applies to Apex, while reuse only applies to Flow
questions.explain: Modularity is a structural property of how a solution is broken apart; reuse is about whether those modular pieces are actually consumed more than once -- a modular solution with nothing reusing its pieces realizes no reuse payoff.

questions.q: What is an invocable Apex method, and why is it useful for reuse?
options: An Apex method exposed so it can be called directly from Flow, letting logic that's awkward to build declaratively be triggered from multiple Flows without reimplementing it each time
An Apex method that can only run once per org
A method that automatically converts Flow logic into Apex
A deprecated feature no longer supported on the platform
questions.explain: Invocable Apex methods bridge Flow and Apex, letting complex or hard-to-express logic be built once in Apex and reused across multiple declarative automations.

questions.q: What is 'premature abstraction,' as this lesson defines it?
options: Building the simplest possible version of a feature with no regard for future needs
Refusing to ever reuse any logic across multiple Flows
A Salesforce term for exceeding governor limits
Over-engineering a generic, flexible, reusable version of something before a second real use case actually demonstrates the need for that flexibility
questions.explain: Premature abstraction pays the cost of generality -- more complexity, more configuration, more edge cases -- for a speculative future need that hasn't actually been demonstrated by a real second use case yet.

questions.q: What practical rule does this lesson give for when to actually build something as a reusable component?
options: Always build everything as reusable and configurable from the very first requirement
Build the specific solution first; refactor it into a reusable piece once a second, real use case actually appears and the shared logic becomes concretely visible
Never build anything reusable under any circumstances
Reuse should only ever be decided by a developer, never an architect
questions.explain: The lesson's practical rule is to build specifically first and refactor toward reuse once a genuine second use case demonstrates the shared need -- not to speculatively build generic structures before that need is real.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what real cost does every reuse decision carry, even when it's the right call?
options: Reuse has no real cost once implemented
Reuse always requires purchasing additional Salesforce licenses
A shared component now has more than one caller depending on its exact behavior, so any future change to it has to be checked against every consumer, not just the one that prompted the change
Shared Apex methods cannot be covered by unit tests
questions.explain: The lesson frames reuse honestly as a trade-off: once something is shared, every future change has a wider blast radius across all its callers, which is worthwhile for genuinely shared, stable logic but risky when forced onto only superficially similar logic.
